title: Thermodynamic Geometry of an Ideal Quon Gas
authors: Leila Yousefzadeh, Hosein Mohammadzadeh, Habib Esmaili, Zahra Ebadi, Morteza Nattagh Najafi
abstract: We investigate the equilibrium thermodynamics and thermodynamic Riemannian geometry of an ideal quon gas within the grand canonical ensemble. By incorporating the algebraic deformation parameter $q$, the system generalizes standard bosonic behavior while recovering the conventional ideal Bose gas in the undeformed limit. A rigorous examination of the ground-state occupation reveals two disconnected mathematical domains of the fugacity. By enforcing thermodynamic continuity, single-valuedness, and consistency with the high-temperature classical limit, we exclude the second mathematical branch and establish the lower interval as the unique physically admissible state space. This identifies the deformation parameter as an intrinsic, generalized Bose--Einstein condensation threshold. Employing the Fisher-Rao metric on the equilibrium parameter manifold, we probe the thermodynamic scalar curvature across all temperature regimes. The scalar curvature remains strictly positive throughout the physical domain, confirming that the deformation preserves an effectively attractive statistical interaction without inducing fermionic tendencies. Near the critical condensation threshold, the curvature increases sharply and exhibits a definitive divergence, providing an unambiguous geometric signature of macroscopic coherence and critical fluctuations. Below the transition temperature, the pinning of fugacity eliminates a fluctuating degree of freedom, collapsing the scalar curvature to zero.
summary: This work develops a thermodynamic and geometric framework for an ideal quon gas, a generalization of bosonic systems. By analyzing the Fisher-Rao metric, the authors show that the scalar curvature provides a clear geometric signature for the Bose-Einstein condensation transition. The curvature diverges at the critical point and vanishes in the condensed phase, confirming the physical interpretation of the quon deformation parameter.
main_problem: The paper investigates the equilibrium thermodynamics and the associated Riemannian geometry of an ideal quon gas.
main_result: The thermodynamic scalar curvature remains strictly positive, confirming an effectively attractive interaction, and exhibits a definitive divergence at the critical condensation threshold, while vanishing below it.
method: The analysis employs the grand canonical ensemble, calculates thermodynamic quantities using generalized polylogarithms, and applies the Fisher-Rao metric to determine the scalar curvature of the state space.
model_or_system: The system is an ideal quon gas, which generalizes standard bosonic behavior via a deformation parameter $q$. The model is analyzed in the grand canonical ensemble, using a generalized occupation number $\langle n_p angle$.
key_observables: Thermodynamic scalar curvature ($R$), average occupation number ($\langle n_p angle$), and the chemical potential ($\mu$).
important_parameters: The deformation parameter $q$, the fugacity ($z$), and the reduced temperature ($T/T_c$).
main_assumptions: The physical state space is restricted by enforcing thermodynamic continuity and single-valuedness, leading to the exclusion of mathematical branches.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the average occupation number for different $q$, the ground-state occupation number showing poles at $z=q$ and $z=1/q$, and the scalar curvature $R$ vs. temperature/fugacity, showing divergence at $T_c$ and zero below $T_c$.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the model and calculates the grand potential. It then analyzes the ground-state occupation to define the physically admissible fugacity domain ($0 < z \le q$). Finally, it constructs the thermodynamic metric and calculates the scalar curvature $R$ across different temperature regimes, linking geometric features to phase transitions.
why_interesting: The use of geometric tools (Riemannian curvature) to characterize phase transitions (like BEC) provides a powerful, universal diagnostic tool for many-body quantum systems, extending beyond standard thermodynamic potentials.
